headline: Cooling has become critical infrastructure in three industries at once
deck: Buildings, data centres and industrial processes are all asking the same grid for heat rejection, and the answers differ by sector.
excerpt: Cooling sets the Gulf's electricity peak, and it is now being demanded by three different loads with three different profiles. That is a grid problem, an equipment problem and a water problem simultaneously.
content:
Air conditioning has always been the Gulf's dominant electrical load. What has changed is that it is no longer only air conditioning.

Three distinct demands for heat rejection now sit on the same infrastructure, and they behave differently enough that treating them as one category is misleading.

The first is buildings, which is the traditional load. It is seasonal, peaks in the afternoon, and follows occupancy. Its growth follows construction, and with a Saudi construction market worth roughly $142.30bn growing at about 3.6 per cent in real terms, that growth is steady rather than dramatic.

The second is industrial process cooling, which is not seasonal at all. A petrochemical plant, a desalination train or a food processing line rejects heat continuously at a rate set by throughput, and its cooling requirement is a process variable rather than a comfort one.

The third is new, and it is the one changing the arithmetic. Data centre cooling is continuous, insensitive to season, concentrated at single points, and rising fast. Saudi data centre load stood near 467 megawatts in the first quarter against pipelines quoted in gigawatts, and every megawatt of information technology load is close to a megawatt of heat that has to leave the building.

Each of the three has a different engineering answer. Buildings are served by chillers and air distribution, with district cooling where density justifies the network. Process cooling uses cooling towers, air-cooled exchangers and once-through seawater at coastal sites. High-density computing has moved past air entirely, to liquid distribution at the rack.

What they share is the constraint. All three reject heat into an ambient that is hot for much of the year, which reduces the efficiency of every method, and all three draw electricity from networks whose peak is already set by cooling.

They also share a water question, and it is the sharpest trade-off in the region. Evaporative cooling is significantly more efficient and consumes water, which in the Gulf is largely desalinated and therefore itself electricity-intensive. Dry cooling consumes no water and more power. Choosing between them is choosing which scarce resource to spend, and the answer differs by site, by season and by who is paying for what.

The equipment consequences run through everything the region is buying. Chillers, pumps, valves, heat exchangers, controls, insulation and now liquid cooling distribution are all in demand simultaneously from three sectors that used to buy at different times.

That convergence was visible across the month's exhibitions without being named: HVACR at the Riyadh construction show, heat exchangers at the static equipment show in Al Khobar, and the cooling content on the Dubai energy floor are three views of the same problem.
author: Jakson Gudawela
seoTitle: Cooling is critical infrastructure in three industries at once
seoDescription: Buildings, data centres and industrial processes all reject heat into the same hot ambient and draw from the same grid, with different answers by sector.
